usage: the default compliment; 좋다 here means clear and healthy, not merely 'good'
건조하다 (乾燥) is the set adjective for dry skin, never 마르다
a borrowed phrase Koreans use for acne and irritation as a noun
note the particle 에 (to/for the skin), the standard frame for skincare claims
examples: 언니 피부가 정말 좋아요.
Your skin is really nice.
a stock compliment; mark the topic with 가, the thing praised
겨울에는 피부가 너무 건조해서 로션을 발라요.
In winter my skin gets so dry that I put on lotion.
건조해서 (because dry) links cause to action with -아서
햇볕에 오래 있었더니 피부가 따갑고 빨개졌어요.
After being in the sun a long time my skin stings and turned red.
빨개지다 = 빨갛다 + 지다, 'become red'; the ㅎ-irregular drops in 빨개
nuance: 피부 is the skin as a surface and a beauty concern, so it overwhelmingly turns up in compliments (피부가 좋다 = clear, glowing) and skincare talk (피부에 좋다, 피부 트러블, 피부가 건조하다). The near-synonym 살 also means 'skin/flesh' but refers to the soft fleshy meat under the surface and to body fat (살이 찌다 = gain weight), so 손등 살이 텄어요 is the chapped flesh while 피부 관리 is the cosmetic surface — never swap them. 피부 is Sino-Korean, 皮膚 'hide-skin', which is why it sounds slightly clinical yet is perfectly everyday. The classic English-speaker trap is reaching for 마르다 ('dry up, become thin') for dry skin; skin takes the adjective 건조하다 instead, and 'I have sensitive skin' is 피부가 예민해요/민감해요, not a 직역 with 'sensitive' as a noun.

Translating 'skin and bones' or 'get under my skin' literally. Those English idioms don't exist in Korean; describe the meaning instead (e.g. 너무 말랐어요 for very thin).
Using 살 when you mean the cosmetic surface. 얼굴 살이 좋아요 sounds like 'nice facial flesh/cheeks'; for clear complexion say 얼굴 피부가 좋아요.

usage: 부러지다 is the verb reserved for snapping long rigid things like bones and branches
튼튼하다 = sturdy/robust; the go-to word for healthy bones, not 강하다
note 에 (for the bones); the frame used in food and calcium ads
an idiom for being extremely thin or worn out
examples: 강아지가 뼈를 좋아해요.
The puppy likes bones.
a simple object sentence; 뼈를 takes the object particle
넘어져서 팔 뼈가 부러졌어요.
I fell and broke the bone in my arm.
부러지다 is intransitive — the bone breaks 'by itself', so use 가
나이가 들면 뼈가 약해져서 칼슘을 챙겨 먹어야 해요.
As you age your bones weaken, so you should take calcium.
약해지다 'become weak' + 챙겨 먹다 'make sure to eat'
nuance: 뼈 is the hard bone inside the body and, by extension, a bone in meat or fish. The crucial collocation is 뼈가 부러지다 'a bone breaks': Korean fusses over WHICH break-verb you use — 부러지다 is for snapping rigid long things (bones, pencils, branches), 깨지다 is for shattering brittle things (glass, plates, a skull as 두개골), and 금이 가다 is a hairline crack/fracture. So a clean break is 부러지다, but a fracture a doctor sees on an X-ray is often 뼈에 금이 갔어요. Native, non-Sino word, so it feels plain and bodily; the formal medical counterpart is 골(骨), seen in compounds like 골절 'fracture' and 골다공증 'osteoporosis'. English speakers misfire by saying 뼈가 깨졌어요 (sounds like the bone shattered into pieces) for an ordinary break — use 부러졌어요.

mistakes: Saying 뼈가 깨졌어요 for a normal broken bone. 깨지다 implies shattering brittle objects; a snapped bone is 부러졌어요. Reserve 금이 갔어요 for a hairline fracture.
Using 강하다 for strong bones. 강하다 fits force or personality; healthy sturdy bones take 튼튼하다, so say 뼈가 튼튼해요.
Forgetting 부러지다 is intransitive and adding 를. Don't say 뼈를 부러뜨렸어요 unless you mean someone actively broke it; for 'my bone broke' say 뼈가 부러졌어요.

usage: 뭉치다 'to clump/lump together' is the set verb for a stiff, knotted muscle
생기다 'come into being'; the natural way to say muscle has appeared
풀다 'to release/undo'; used for stretching out tension, opposite of 뭉치다
근육통 (筋肉痛) is the noun for the soreness after a workout
examples: 저 사람은 근육이 많아요.
That person has a lot of muscle.
describing build; 많다 'be many/much' takes 가 on the thing
어제 운동을 무리해서 오늘 온몸 근육이 아파요.
I overdid the workout yesterday so today my muscles ache all over.
무리하다 'to overdo it' + 온몸 'whole body'
오래 앉아 있었더니 어깨 근육이 뭉쳐서 좀 풀어 줬어요.
After sitting a long time my shoulder muscles knotted up, so I worked them loose.
뭉치다 ↔ 풀다 pairing; 줬어요 here adds a gentle 'did for it' nuance
nuance: 근육 is muscle tissue, the body part you build at the gym and the thing that gets sore or knotted. It is Sino-Korean, 筋肉 'sinew-flesh', which is why the soreness noun is 근육통 (筋肉痛, lit. muscle-pain). The signature collocation is 근육이 뭉치다 'the muscle clumps up' — 뭉치다 literally means to lump together (rice 뭉치다 into a ball), and a stiff knotted muscle is pictured the same way; its natural opposite is 근육을 풀다 'release the muscle' by stretching. Don't confuse 근육 (the tissue) with 힘 (strength/power, the force it produces): 힘이 세다 = strong, but 근육이 많다 = muscular. The English-speaker pitfall is describing a knot as 딱딱하다 'hard' — that just states a texture; the idiomatic medical-feeling phrase Koreans actually say is 근육이 뭉쳤어요.

Mixing up 근육 and 힘. 근육이 세요 is wrong; for 'I'm strong' say 힘이 세요, and reserve 근육이 많아요 for being muscular.
Saying 근육을 키워요 expecting it to mean a quick 'flex'. 키우다 means to grow/raise muscle over time (training); to flex a muscle right now is 힘을 줘요 or 알통을 만들어요.

usage: 뛰다 'to run/leap' doubles as 'to beat' for the heart
두근거리다 is the onomatopoeic verb for a fast, fluttering heartbeat
약하다 'be weak'; a standard medical description
심장마비 (心臟痲痺) lit. 'heart paralysis', the medical term
examples: 사람은 심장이 하나예요.
People have one heart.
a simple fact sentence; 하나 'one' + 예요
갑자기 뒤에서 불러서 심장이 멎는 줄 알았어요.
Someone suddenly called from behind and I thought my heart would stop.
멎다 'to stop/cease'; -는 줄 알았다 'I thought it would'
계단을 뛰어 올라왔더니 심장이 터질 것 같아요.
I ran up the stairs and now my heart feels like it'll burst.
터지다 'to burst'; vivid but everyday exaggeration for racing
nuance: 심장 is the physical heart organ — the muscle that beats — and it is Sino-Korean, 心臟 'heart-organ'. The key boundary for English speakers: in Korean the SEAT OF EMOTION is not 심장. Love, sincerity and feelings live in 마음 (the mind-heart, 마음이 아프다 = heartbroken) or 가슴 (the chest, 가슴이 뛰다/벅차다 for excitement and emotion). 심장 stays literal and medical: it 뛰다 (beats), 두근거리다 (pounds with adrenaline or fear), or 멎다/터지다 in vivid shock. Note 심장 vs 가슴: a doctor checks your 심장, but you clutch your 가슴 (chest) in feeling. The classic 직역 trap is writing 'my heart aches (emotionally)' as 심장이 아파요 — that sounds like cardiac pain; for emotional hurt say 마음이 아파요.

Translating 'from the bottom of my heart' as 심장. The idiom is 진심으로 or 마음 깊은 곳에서, never with 심장.

usage: 검사 (檢査) 'examination'; this compound is the standard hospital term
혈액형 (血液型) lit. 'blood-type'; the everyday word even in casual chat
뽑다 'to pull out/draw'; the verb for drawing blood or pulling teeth
순환 (循環) 'circulation'; common in health talk, e.g. 혈액 순환이 잘 돼요
examples: 저는 혈액형이 A형이에요.
My blood type is A.
the one casual spot 혈액 appears daily; 혈액형 + 이에요
건강 검진에서 혈액을 뽑았어요.
They drew blood at my health checkup.
건강 검진 'health screening'; 뽑다 for the draw
손발이 찬 건 혈액 순환이 잘 안 돼서 그래요.
Cold hands and feet happen because circulation isn't good.
혈액 순환이 안 되다 'circulation doesn't work well'
nuance: 혈액 is the formal, clinical word for blood — Sino-Korean 血液 'blood-fluid' — so it lives in hospital and health vocabulary: 혈액 검사 (blood test), 혈액형 (blood type), 혈액 순환 (circulation), 혈액 기증 (blood donation). Its everyday counterpart is the native word 피, which is what you say for blood you actually SEE: a bleeding cut is 피가 나요, never 혈액이 나요. So the dividing line is register and visibility — 피 = the red liquid in daily life, 혈액 = the technical substance in medical contexts. The one exception where the Sino word wins in casual speech is 혈액형 'blood type', which almost everyone says over 피의 형. The English-speaker pitfall is using 혈액 for ordinary bleeding (sounds like a lab report) — for a nosebleed or a scrape, say 피.

Mixing up the verbs. You don't 마시다 or 흘리다 혈액 in normal speech; blood is 뽑다 (drawn) or 검사하다 (tested), while you 흘리다 피 (shed blood).

usage: 뱉다 'to spit out'; the set verb, used literally and in 'spit it out (confess)'
삼키다 'to swallow'; also used for swallowing words/anger
고이다 'to pool/collect'; what your mouth does at a tasty smell
침이 마르다 'mouth goes dry'; idiom for praising someone endlessly
examples: 아기가 침을 흘려요.
The baby is drooling.
흘리다 'to let flow'; simple everyday drooling
길에 침을 뱉으면 안 돼요.
You mustn't spit on the street.
manners; -으면 안 되다 'must not'
맛있는 냄새를 맡으니까 입에 침이 고여요.
Smelling the delicious food makes my mouth water.
Korean's exact equivalent of 'mouth waters' = 침이 고이다
nuance: 침 is the saliva in your mouth, and it pairs with a precise set of verbs: 침을 뱉다 (spit out), 침을 삼키다 (swallow), 침을 흘리다 (drool), and 침이 고이다 (pool — the 'mouth waters' image). Beware the homonyms: this same syllable 침 also means an acupuncture needle (침을 맞다 = get acupuncture), a (clock/compass) needle/hand, and 'sting'(벌침 = bee sting) — context fully disambiguates, but it surprises learners. Two vivid idioms ride on it: 침이 마르도록 칭찬하다 'praise until your mouth runs dry' and 군침이 돌다 'mouth waters with craving'. The pitfall is the verb: English 'water' (as in mouth-watering) tempts a 직역 with 물, but Korean says 침이 고이다 (saliva pools), and 'I'm drooling' is 침을 흘려요, not anything with 물.

Wrong verb for drooling. 침이 나와요 is understandable but flat; natural Korean is 침을 흘려요 for drooling.

usage: 흘리다 'to shed'; literal sweating AND the idiom for hard effort
나다 'to come out/occur'; the most everyday way to say you're sweating
닦다 'to wipe/clean'; with a towel or sleeve
식은땀 lit. 'cooled sweat'; the sweat of fear, nausea, or close calls
examples: 더워서 땀이 나요.
It's hot so I'm sweating.
the basic frame; 땀이 나다 with 가 on the spontaneous event
운동하고 나서 수건으로 땀을 닦았어요.
After exercising I wiped off the sweat with a towel.
-고 나서 'after doing'; 닦다 takes 를
발표 직전이라 손에 식은땀이 났어요.
Right before the presentation I broke out in a cold sweat.
식은땀이 나다 = the fear/nerves version of sweating
nuance: 땀 is sweat, a native word, and the verb choice carries the meaning. 땀이 나다 (sweat occurs) is the neutral everyday 'I'm sweating', while 땀을 흘리다 (shed sweat) both describes heavy sweating AND works as a metaphor for hard work — 땀 흘려 일하다 'to work by the sweat of one's brow', and 노력의 땀 'the sweat of effort'. A key compound is 식은땀 'cold sweat', the clammy sweat of fear, illness, or a near-miss (식은땀이 나다/흐르다). Contrast 땀 with 눈물 (tears) and 침 (saliva): all three are bodily fluids that idiomatically 나다, but only 땀 carries the 'effort/labor' connotation. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'sweat' as a verb and saying 땀을 해요 — Korean has no 'to sweat' verb; you either 흘리다 the sweat or it 나다 on its own.

Missing the idiom. 땀을 흘리다 can mean hard work, so 땀 흘려 번 돈 means 'money earned through hard work', not literally sweaty money.
Using plain 땀 for the fear-sweat. The clammy nervous kind is specifically 식은땀, e.g. 식은땀이 났어요, not just 땀이 났어요.

usage: tears come / I start to cry
나다 'to come out'; the most natural way to say tears well up
흘리다 'to let flow'; slightly more vivid/literary than 나다
describing a person, not a quantity of liquid
참다 'to endure/hold in'; fighting off crying
examples: 슬픈 영화를 봐서 눈물이 나요.
I'm tearing up because I watched a sad movie.
cause + 눈물이 나다; the spontaneous event takes 가
하품을 했더니 눈물이 핑 돌았어요.
I yawned and tears welled up in my eyes.
눈물이 핑 돌다 = tears suddenly well up; 핑 is the swirl mimetic
울고 싶었지만 사람들 앞이라 눈물을 꾹 참았어요.
I wanted to cry but I held the tears back hard in front of people.
꾹 참다 'endure firmly'; 눈물을 참다 takes the object 를
nuance: 눈물 is tears, a transparent native compound 눈(eye)+물(water). Its default verb is 눈물이 나다 'tears come' — note that 'I cry' is often expressed this way (눈물이 나요 ≈ 'I'm tearing up') rather than only with the verb 울다 'to cry/weep'. 눈물을 흘리다 'shed tears' is a touch more vivid, and 눈물을 참다 means to hold them back. Watch the idiom 눈물이 많다: it does NOT mean you produce a lot of liquid — it means you're a soft-hearted person who cries easily; its opposite 눈물이 없다 means stoic. Vivid set phrases: 눈물이 핑 돌다 (tears suddenly well), 눈물이 그렁그렁하다 (eyes brimming). The pitfall is the 직역 눈물을 울어요 — you can't 'cry tears' in Korean; tears 나다 (come) or you 흘리다 (shed) them, while 울다 stands alone as 'to cry'.

Vivid set phrases: 눈물이 핑 돌다 (tears suddenly well), 눈물이 그렁그렁하다 (eyes brimming).
A transparent native compound 눈(eye)+물(water).
The pitfall is the 직역 눈물을 울어요 — you can't 'cry tears' in Korean; tears 나다 (come) or you 흘리다 (shed) them, while 울다 stands alone as 'to cry'.

mistakes: Saying 눈물을 울어요. 울다 already means 'to cry' and takes no object; say 눈물이 나요 (tears come) or just 울어요.
Literalizing 눈물이 많아요 as 'lots of tear liquid'. It describes a tender person who cries easily, like English 'a crybaby/soft-hearted'.
Wrong particle on the spontaneous event. 'Tears came' is 눈물이 났어요 (가), not 눈물을 났어요; the object 를 only fits 흘리다/참다.

usage: 쉬다 — the SAME verb as 'to rest'; 숨을 쉬다 = 'breathe'
차다 'to fill up'; the set phrase for being winded
참다 'to hold in/endure'; also used for holding back emotion
I take a deep breath in
들이쉬다 'breathe in' vs 내쉬다 'breathe out', built on 쉬다
examples: 천천히 숨을 쉬어 보세요.
Try breathing slowly.
clinic instruction; -아 보세요 'try doing'
계단을 뛰어 올라왔더니 숨이 차요.
I ran up the stairs and now I'm out of breath.
숨이 차다 — winded; the event takes 가
물속에서 30초 동안 숨을 참았어요.
I held my breath for 30 seconds underwater.
숨을 참다 takes the object 를; 동안 'for (a duration)'
nuance: 숨 is a breath / one's breathing, a native word, and its core verb is 숨을 쉬다 'to breathe' — note that 쉬다 is also the verb 'to rest', a neat overlap (breathing is the body resting). Directional variants build on it: 들이쉬다 (breathe in), 내쉬다 (breathe out), 한숨을 쉬다 (sigh). To say you're winded, Korean uses 숨이 차다 'breath fills up' (the event takes 가), and to hold your breath is 숨을 참다. Compare 숨 with the Sino-Korean 호흡 (呼吸 'exhale-inhale'), which is the technical 'respiration' used in yoga, medicine, and 인공호흡 (CPR) — 숨 is the plain everyday word. Vivid idioms: 숨이 막히다 'be suffocated/overwhelmed', 숨을 거두다 'to pass away (lit. gather one's breath)'. The pitfall is saying 숨을 해요 — there's no 'to breath' verb; you 쉬다 (do/rest) the breath.

Wrong particle for being winded. 'I'm out of breath' is 숨이 차요 (가); don't say 숨을 차요. Use 를 only with 참다 (hold).

usage: 기르다 'to grow/raise'; the verb for growing hair, beards, pets
깎다 'to shave/pare'; same verb as shaving and sharpening a pencil
나다 'to grow/sprout'; how facial/body hair appears
콧(nose)수염 vs 턱(chin)수염 specify which when it matters
examples: 고양이는 수염이 있어요.
Cats have whiskers.
수염 also = animal whiskers; simple 있다 sentence
아빠는 매일 아침 수염을 깎아요.
Dad shaves every morning.
daily routine; 깎다 takes 를
한동안 면도를 안 했더니 수염이 덥수룩하게 났어요.
I didn't shave for a while so a scruffy beard grew in.
덥수룩하다 'be bushy/scruffy'; 수염이 나다 for it coming in
nuance: 수염 covers all facial hair — beard and mustache together — and also animal whiskers (고양이 수염), so context tells you which; to be specific Koreans add a body part: 콧수염 (mustache, nose-beard), 턱수염 (chin beard), 구레나룻 (sideburns). It's Sino-Korean, 鬚髥. The verbs are the heart of it: you 기르다 (grow) a beard over time, it 나다 (sprouts) on its own, and you 깎다 (shave) it off — 깎다 is the same verb as shaving hair short and sharpening a pencil, picturing paring something down. Note the everyday near-synonym 면도(面刀)하다 'to shave' (lit. 'face-blade'): 면도하다 is the act of shaving, while 수염을 깎다 names the beard as object. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 자르다 'to cut' — you cut hair with scissors (머리를 자르다), but a beard is pared/shaved with 깎다, not 잘라요.

Using 자라다 transitively for growing a beard. 자라다 'to grow' is intransitive (수염이 자라요 = it grows); to deliberately grow one say 수염을 길러요.

usage: 생기다 'to form/appear'; the set verb for wrinkles coming with age
자글자글 is the mimetic word for lots of tiny crinkly wrinkles
펴다 'to unfold/straighten'; for skin or ironing cloth
눈가 'eye area'; the most-mentioned wrinkle spot
examples: 할머니는 주름이 많아요.
Grandma has many wrinkles.
appearance; 많다 takes 가 on 주름
웃을 때 눈가에 주름이 살짝 생겨요.
When I smile, slight wrinkles form around my eyes.
눈가에 'at the eye area' + 살짝 'slightly'
다림질을 해서 셔츠 주름을 폈어요.
I ironed out the wrinkles in the shirt.
same 주름 for cloth creases; 펴다 removes them
nuance: 주름 means a wrinkle on skin AND a fold/crease in fabric or paper — same word for both. It's a native word, and its defining verb is 주름이 생기다 'wrinkles form' (생기다 = come into being), the standard way to talk about aging skin; you smooth them with 주름을 펴다 (unfold/straighten, also used for ironing). Common spots: 눈가 주름 (crow's feet), 이마 주름 (forehead lines), 팔자 주름 (nasolabial folds, named for the 八 shape). A vivid mimetic, 자글자글하다, describes finely crinkled skin. Don't confuse 주름 (a line/fold in a surface) with 흉터 (a scar from a wound) or 점 (a mole) — different skin features entirely. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb: 'wrinkles appear' tempts 주름이 나다 (the 나다 you'd use for pimples or sweat), but wrinkles specifically 생기다 — say 주름이 생겼어요.

usage: 빼다 'to take out/remove'; the set verb for laser mole removal
있다 'to exist'; describing where a mole sits
I draw on a beauty spot
찍다 'to dot/stamp'; making a point, also photos and dipping sauce
examples: 얼굴에 점이 하나 있어요.
I have one mole on my face.
appearance; 하나 'one' counts it
눈 밑에 있는 점을 병원에서 뺐어요.
I had the mole under my eye removed at a clinic.
점을 빼다; 눈 밑 'under the eye'
선생님이 칠판에 점을 찍었어요.
The teacher made a dot on the board.
same 점 = 'dot/point'; 찍다 for marking it
nuance: 점 is a mole on the skin, and the very same word means a dot, point, spot, period (punctuation), and even a 'point' as in a score or aspect (좋은 점 = a good point). It's Sino-Korean, 點. For a skin mole the defining collocation is 점을 빼다 'remove the mole' — 빼다 means to take/pull out (also used for 'lose weight', 살을 빼다), reflecting how a mole is extracted by laser. Don't use 지우다 'to erase' (that's for writing, stains, or files) — you 빼다 a mole, not 지워요. Useful relatives: 주근깨 (freckles), 기미 (age/sun spots, melasma). Beware the homonym range: 점심 (點心, lunch) literally 'dot the heart', 점수 (點數, score), 점 보다 (have one's fortune told). The English-speaker pitfall is calling a mole a 'spot' and erasing it — Korean removes (빼다) the 점.
